clue.text: Play in twisted tree sporting something on your head

indicators.note: a piece that goes in something is buried between its letters instead of being added at either end

parts.note: the thing you sport on your head, and it opens up after two of its three letters

indicators.note: a tree twisted right round hands its letters back the other way, last one first

parts.note: the elm is the crossword's short tree, and it goes in the other way round

explanation.walkthrough: 'Play in twisted tree' reads as an actor performing up a trunk. The definition stops after the very first word, and everything after it is instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Play -> HAMLET: the general word points at one famous instance, Shakespeare's tragedy of the Danish prince.

clue.text: Virtuous, with passion, but no heart

indicators.note: the heart of a word is the letter sitting at its centre, and taking it away lets the two halves close up

parts.note: doing something with passion is doing it hotly
the middle letter of that five-letter word is a T, and it is what goes

explanation.walkthrough: The surface offers a passionate but heartless lover. In the parse 'heart' is a position rather than a feeling, and the comma marks where the definition stops.
explanation.definitionFit: Virtuous -> HOLY: both name moral goodness, with the answer carrying the religious weight of it, a saint's virtue rather than mere decency.

clue.text: Something clicked with inspirational person, inspiring love

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so whatever inspires takes the next piece into itself

parts.note: the muse is the classical figure who supplies an artist with ideas
love is a score of nothing at tennis, written as a round O

explanation.walkthrough: 'Inspirational' and 'inspiring' come from the same root and the clue leans on that: one of them is a synonym to be converted, the other an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Something clicked with -> MOUSE: the desk device you press to click, named by the action it performs rather than by its shape or its tail.

clue.text: Taxi covered in melted cheese and spicy marinade

indicators.note: something covered in a substance has that substance all round it, so the vehicle ends up enclosed
cheese that has melted has run out of its own shape, and letters treated that way keep none of their order

parts.note: the same six letters in a new order, splitting either side of the vehicle
a cab is a taxi, three letters landing in the middle

explanation.walkthrough: Every other word in the surface is food, which makes 'Taxi' the odd one out and the place to start: it is the only thing here nobody would eat.
explanation.definitionFit: spicy marinade -> ESCABECHE: the Spanish and Latin American dish of fried fish steeped in vinegar and paprika, named after the steeping liquid.

clue.text: Warm, new filling cooked with the last bits of special pastry

indicators.note: a filling sits inside whatever it fills, so the letter lands between the others rather than beside them

parts.note: food cooked in a pan has been fried, and the word opens up before its final letter
n is the standard abbreviation for new

indicators.note: the last bit of a word is the letter it finishes on, taken here from each of the two words named after it

parts.note: speciaL and pastrY each give up the letter they end on, in that order

explanation.walkthrough: 'Warm, new filling cooked' reads as a pie straight from the oven, which is exactly how the definition hides: 'Warm' on its own is the whole of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Warm -> FRIENDLY: the sense used of a person's manner, a warm welcome from a warm host, not a temperature.

clue.text: Mix the tips of asparagus, radish, radicchio and dried pulses

definitions.note: The definition is plural where the answer names one device: it is being defined by the train of radio pulses it sends out and listens for.

indicators.note: mixing ingredients leaves none of them where it started, which is what happens to these letters
the tip of a word is the letter it starts with, taken from every word in the list, the little joining word included

parts.note: five words, each handing over the letter it opens with, in the order they are listed

explanation.walkthrough: The list reads like a salad, and the 'and' is fodder alongside the vegetables — setters count it as a word like any other, which is what makes the letters come out.
explanation.definitionFit: pulses -> RADAR: it works by firing short bursts of radio energy and timing the echoes, so the definition names it by those bursts.

clue.text: Each sufferer originally put on drugs gets better

indicators.note: the origin of a word is the letter it starts with, and that single letter is all this hands over

parts.note: ea is the shopkeeper's abbreviation for each, as on a price list

indicators.note: in a down entry whatever is put on something is written above it, so these letters sit on top of the drugs

parts.note: the first letter of the word, and nothing else of it
E is ecstasy, so a plural of them is ES

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a patient on medication and 'gets better' finishes it so smoothly that it never looks like a definition sitting at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: gets better -> EASES: said of a pain or a symptom that lessens, the intransitive sense rather than a person recovering.

clue.text: Dozer's head with fantastic realm inside? That's it!

definitions.text: Dozer's head with fantastic realm inside? That's it!

indicators.note: something fantastic is wildly out of the ordinary, so the realm's letters are not left in the order they arrived in
a piece put inside an assembly is buried within it, not joined on at either end

parts.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so the sleeper gives up a D
the same five letters, shaken into another order
'with' and 'and' both join two things, so one can be written for the other

explanation.walkthrough: An all-in-one: the sentence describes the place and builds it at the same time, and 'with' works twice over, as joinery in the surface and as three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: the country a sleeping head wanders into, imaginary and marvellous, which 'That's it!' then points at.

clue.text: Key is faulty I'm afraid

indicators.note: a faulty thing does not work as it should, and faulty letters will not stay in the order handed to you

parts.note: the anagram fodder, five letters including the little verb

explanation.walkthrough: 'Key is faulty' sounds like a complaint about a lock or a piano, and the trap is reading 'Key' as the definition when it is the raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: I'm afraid -> YIKES: the cry let out on being startled, so the definition is fright spoken aloud rather than a polite apology.

clue.text: Countdown supporter's vigorous handclap taking in the final vowel

indicators.note: clapping done vigorously is loose and violent, and letters treated that way stay nowhere near where they were
what is taken in is absorbed into the middle of the assembly rather than tacked onto an end

parts.note: the anagram fodder, eight letters
the vowels run A, E, I, O, U, so the last of them is a U

explanation.walkthrough: The italics make Countdown the television programme and its fans. The countdown that matters is the one before a rocket leaves the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Countdown supporter -> LAUNCH PAD: the platform holding a rocket upright while the seconds are counted off, so 'supporter' is meant physically.

clue.text: Mature boy holding up a boring PC game

indicators.note: in a down entry whatever does the holding up is underneath, propping up everything written above it
to bore is to drill into something, so the letter described that way ends up inside

parts.note: two letters taken at face value, and they come apart
the article at face value, one letter drilled into the middle
a boy who has matured is a man

explanation.walkthrough: The whole sentence reads as a mugging in an amusement arcade. Every word of it is instruction except the last, and that last word is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: game -> PACMAN: definition by example, the maze-chase arcade machine of 1980 standing in for the general word.

clue.text: Grass snake's tail moved

indicators.note: the tail of a word is its last letter, and being told it has moved means the letters no longer stand in the order given

parts.note: the five letters of the reptile, with only the final one changing place

explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass snake' is one creature in the surface and two jobs in the parse: the definition stops after the first word and the reptile is raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: Grass -> SNEAK: both are British slang for telling on somebody — a grass informs on you, and a sneak is the schoolyard version.

clue.text: Self-driving car that is made to leave, leaves

definitions.note: The definition is plural and the answer singular: what you cook with is the leaves themselves, used by the handful rather than one at a time.

indicators.note: being made to leave is being sent out, so those two letters are taken away from what was holding them

parts.note: the Volkswagen Beetle with a mind of its own from the Disney films
i.e. is Latin id est, 'that is', and these are the two letters shown the door

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that 'leave' and 'leaves' sit a word apart meaning different things: one is an eviction, the other is what you chop into a sauce.
explanation.definitionFit: leaves -> HERB: the leaves of a plant kept for flavour, so a jar of basil or thyme is exactly what the word names.

clue.text: Stupidly rich, devoted man joins mother and sons for feast-day

indicators.note: doing something stupidly is doing it with no care for where things end up, and these letters end up in a new arrangement

parts.note: the four letters of the word, rearranged
a saint is the devoted man, and st is how a saint's name is written
ma is the familiar word for a mother
s is the abbreviation for son, kept singular while the surface talks of several

explanation.walkthrough: Read the opening three words as one description of a wealthy churchgoer and the clue never comes apart. 'Stupidly' belongs to 'rich' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: feast-day -> CHRISTMAS: in the church calendar a feast is a day set aside to mark an event, and December 25 is the greatest of them.

clue.text: The Independent editor is exhausted

parts.note: the paper this puzzle appears in, speaking of itself as us
ed is the short form of editor, as in a letter to the ed

explanation.walkthrough: A setter is allowed to point at his own paper, and the italics are the tell: the title is not there for the surface but to be read as 'we'.
explanation.definitionFit: exhausted -> USED: the sense in 'used up', a supply entirely consumed, rather than a person who is tired out.

clue.text: Application shown by a police constable in tin hat

indicators.note: pieces put in something land between its letters, so the assembly has to open up to take them

parts.note: Sn is the chemical symbol for tin, from the Latin stannum
the word is used as itself, three letters lifted from the clue
the article at face value, one letter
PC is the rank a British bobby holds, printed in front of the name

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tin hat' is a soldier's helmet, which is why it reads as a single thing. The parse needs it as two, and prising the phrase apart is the whole difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: Application -> SNAPCHAT: 'application' is the full word an app is short for, and this photo-messaging one is a famous instance of it.

clue.text: Having dropped diamonds, Danny Ocean's in a state of confusion and anger

indicators.note: what has been dropped is gone, so the letter named goes before anything else is done
letters in confusion are in no settled order at all, which is the instruction to rearrange them

parts.note: d is the card player's abbreviation for the suit, and it is the letter dropped
the name without that letter leaves nine to be rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: Danny Ocean is the thief George Clooney plays in the Ocean's Eleven films, and the diamonds he drops here are a suit of cards rather than loot.
explanation.definitionFit: anger -> ANNOYANCE: the mild end of anger, irritation at something petty rather than rage, which is the sense this noun carries.

clue.text: Schedule the closure of paint factory

parts.note: to schedule something is to plan it

indicators.note: the closure of a word is the letter it shuts with, and only that one letter is wanted

parts.note: the letter that word closes on

explanation.walkthrough: 'The closure of paint factory' reads as a line of industrial news, which is what keeps the last word from looking like the definition it is.
explanation.definitionFit: factory -> PLANT: the industrial sense of the word, the works and machinery of a site, with nothing growing anywhere in it.

clue.text: Dutch cake decorator carrying baked product is a draw for kids

indicators.note: in a down entry whoever does the carrying is underneath the load, so what is carried gets written above them

parts.note: a pie is the baked product, riding on top of everything else
D is the dictionary's abbreviation for Dutch, used in word histories
the one who pipes icing onto a cake

explanation.walkthrough: He led Hamelin's children away behind his pipe, which is the joke in 'a draw for kids' — and the legend is German, so 'Dutch' is only ever a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: a draw for kids -> PIED PIPER: he drew the children out of the town behind him, so 'draw' means both attraction and leading away.

clue.text: Cowdenbeath perhaps to emerge victorious after losing one

indicators.note: what is lost is subtracted, and 'after' says the subtraction happens once the earlier words have handed over their letters

parts.note: to emerge victorious is to win, and the little word in front comes along too
the Roman numeral for one, and this is the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: Cowdenbeath is a small place in Fife, best known outside Scotland for its football club, and 'perhaps' is what turns the name into a general word.
explanation.definitionFit: Cowdenbeath perhaps -> TOWN: definition by example, one Scottish place standing in for the general word, which 'perhaps' politely admits.

clue.text: The beginning or the end of Highlander? Or The Shining?

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is the single letter it opens with, taken here from the film title named after it

parts.note: the opening letter of the title that follows
the little word is lifted straight out of the clue, two letters

indicators.note: the end of a word is the letter it finishes on, taken from that same title

parts.note: the letter that title finishes on
the same two letters again, capitalised here only to start a sentence

explanation.walkthrough: Two films and only one of them defines: Highlander is there to be taken apart letter by letter, while Kubrick's title is an example of the genre.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shining -> HORROR: definition by example, one famous film of the genre standing in for the genre itself.

clue.text: Jig, shake and carouse without stopping

indicators.note: shaking a thing loosens everything in it, so these three letters come out in a different order

parts.note: the three letters of the joining word, shaken into a new order

indicators.note: a stopping is a dentist's filling, and a word without its filling keeps only the letters at its two ends

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word, once the middle has been taken out

explanation.walkthrough: 'Without stopping' reads as carousing all night, and that is the trap: it is not about carrying on but about a filling being removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Jig -> DANCE: a jig is one lively dance, so the particular names the general — and as verbs, to jig about is to dance.

clue.text: Melon that's hard held up by weedy criminal

indicators.note: a thing held up by something rests on it, and that little preposition is what the words hand over
a criminal is crooked, and crooked letters are ones bent out of their proper order

parts.note: H is the grade stamped on a hard pencil
what rests on a support is held up by it, and the preposition is taken as its two letters
the five letters of the word, rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: 'Melon that's hard' sounds like one phrase about unripe fruit. The definition is the first word alone, and 'hard' is already doing wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Melon -> HONEYDEW: the general word points at one variety, the pale green sweet one sold in wedges.

clue.text: My parse's wrong, assuming 2's first letter is M?

indicators.note: letters called wrong are letters out of their proper places, which is the instruction to rearrange them
to assume a thing is to take it on, so the shuffled letters close around the one they take in

parts.note: the anagram fodder, eight letters counting the s of the possessive

indicators.note: the first letter is the one a word opens with, and the numeral has to be spelled out before it can give one

parts.note: write the numeral out as a word and it starts with a T

explanation.walkthrough: '2' looks like a cross-reference, and 2 down really does begin with M, which is the trap. The number wants spelling out instead.
explanation.definitionFit: M? -> SPYMASTER: definition by example, M being the head of the secret service in the Bond books, one particular holder of the job.

clue.text: Jesus repeatedly exposed political figure's lie

indicators.note: exposing a word strips the letters at its two edges, and doing that over and over leaves only what stood at the centre

parts.note: strip the outside letters twice over and a single letter is left standing in the middle
a Tory is a member of the British Conservative party

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has Jesus catching out a politician, which is why nobody looks at the name as five letters waiting to be peeled — twice.
explanation.definitionFit: lie -> STORY: the nursery sense of the word, since telling stories is what a child is told off for when the tale is untrue.

clue.text: I see star chopping out line in front

parts.note: 'ah' is the noise of understanding, the spoken form of 'I see'

indicators.note: chopping something out takes it from the middle of what held it and leaves the rest to close up

parts.note: the star of a film has the lead role
l is the abbreviation for line, as in a reference to a poem, and it is the letter chopped out

explanation.walkthrough: 'I see star' reads as an astronomer's note. Both halves of it are wordplay, and the definition is waiting at the far end of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: in front -> AHEAD: the same position said two ways, since a runner ahead of the field is the one in front of it.

clue.text: Creative works put up in sequence

indicators.note: in a down entry a piece put up is written from the bottom towards the top, so its letters arrive the other way round

parts.note: art is the collective word for creative work, and it goes up the grid
the little word at face value, two letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'In sequence' reads as one phrase and then splits in two: the first word is already letters, and only the second is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: sequence -> TRAIN: a train of thought, or of events, is a sequence of them following one behind another.

clue.text: Last course of Italian meal is left unfinished

indicators.note: a word left unfinished stops short of its final letter, so that letter never gets written down

parts.note: the pasta course comes before the main one at an Italian table

explanation.walkthrough: 'Last course' looks like a single phrase about pudding. The definition is the first word on its own, and the course belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Last -> PAST: the sense in 'the past week', meaning the one just gone, which is exactly what 'last week' says.

clue.text: The woman regularly went to get bed linen

parts.note: the pronoun that stands in for the woman

indicators.note: letters taken regularly are taken at a fixed interval, here every other one across the word that follows

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of the word, the ones an even count picks up

explanation.walkthrough: 'The woman regularly went' reads as a habit, and that is what disguises 'regularly' as a description of her rather than an instruction about letters.
explanation.definitionFit: bed linen -> SHEET: bed linen is the class of cloth a bed is made up with, and this is the main item in it.

clue.text: Move location of screw

definitions.meaning: the small shift someone makes without quite waking, or what a spoon does to soup
in British slang a screw is a prison officer, so the location is the jail he works in

explanation.walkthrough: Four words and no wordplay at all. 'Screw' is not a fastening here, and the second definition is a place rather than an action, which is what hides the join.
explanation.definitionFit: Move -> STIR is the slight movement of a sleeper; location of screw -> STIR is old slang for prison, where a screw is the warder.

clue.text: Snow leopard's attack quietly carried out

indicators.note: something carried out has been taken away from where it was, so the letter named leaves the word

parts.note: a cat's attack is a pounce
p is piano in music, the direction to play quietly, and it is the letter taken away

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is a picture of the animal it names, a big cat pouncing without a sound, which is what makes the definition so hard to see as one.
explanation.definitionFit: Snow leopard -> OUNCE: the old name for that cat of the high Himalaya, a different word entirely from the unit of weight.

clue.text: A British rugby union player's opening try is most unexpected

indicators.note: the opening of a word is the letter it starts with, and that letter is all this part of the clue hands over

parts.note: the article at face value, one letter
B is the abbreviation for British, as in BBC
RU is how the fifteen-a-side code is written on a fixture list
the first letter of player
a test is a try in the sense of a trial or an attempt

explanation.walkthrough: The rugby scene is a decoy: 'try' has to be read as an attempt rather than a score, and the definition is the superlative at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: most unexpected -> ABRUPTEST: something abrupt arrives with no warning, so the superlative is the one that catches you furthest off guard.

clue.text: Admitting defeat, yankee fellow's excused from playing cricket?

parts.note: yankee is Y in the radio alphabet used for spelling names out loud

indicators.note: a player excused from a duty is left out of it, so that letter drops out of the word for the duty

parts.note: the side that is not batting is fielding
f is the abbreviation for fellow, as after the name of a Royal Society member, and it is the letter excused

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is the setter conceding that fielding is only one of the things done at cricket: a part of the game is standing in for all of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Admitting defeat -> YIELDING: to yield is to give in to a stronger force, and the -ing form matches the definition's.

clue.text: Columnist, say, who sets things straight on the radio

indicators.note: words on the radio are heard and never seen, so the answer is spelled the way it sounds rather than the way its sense suggests

parts.note: someone who sets things straight puts them right, which makes them a righter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Columnist, say' looks as though 'say' is the sound instruction. It is the by-example flag, and the real instruction waits at the other end of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Columnist, say -> WRITER: definition by example, since a columnist is one kind of writer and 'say' marks the example.
